questions.question: What is the gold standard for the definitive diagnosis of renal amyloidosis?
options: Kidney biopsy with Congo red stain
questions.explanation: Renal biopsy with Congo red stain is the gold standard, as it demonstrates amyloid deposits with apple-green birefringence under polarized light, confirming the definitive diagnosis.

questions.question: What finding in the kidney biopsy confirms the presence of amyloid?
options: Apple green birefringence with Congo red
questions.explanation: Apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining is characteristic of amyloid, confirming the diagnosis of renal amyloidosis.

questions.question: In renal amyloidosis, Congo red staining is complemented by immunohistochemistry to identify:
options: Immune complexes with C3 and C4
Free light chains (AL) or amyloid A (AA)
questions.explanation: Immunohistochemistry allows differentiating the type of amyloid, being essential for management: identifying AL light chains (associated with myeloma) or AA amyloid (chronic inflammation) guides specific treatment.

questions.question: What is the main usefulness of renal biopsy in suspected systemic amyloidosis?
options: Confirm the diagnosis and type amyloid
questions.explanation: The kidney biopsy not only confirms the presence of amyloid, but through immunohistochemistry or mass spectrometry it typifies the type of amyloid, crucial for deciding the specific treatment.

questions.question: In a patient with nephrotic proteinuria and suspected amyloidosis, renal biopsy is indicated to:
options: Confirm amyloid deposits and classify subtype
questions.explanation: In unexplained nephrotic proteinuria, renal biopsy is the procedure that confirms amyloidosis and allows classifying the subtype (AL vs AA), which defines the prognosis and targeted therapy.

questions.question: What technique additional to light microscopy is used to confirm the type of amyloid in the kidney biopsy?
questions.explanation: La espectrometría de masas en muestras de biopsia renal es el método más preciso para identificar la proteína amiloide específica, superando a la inmunohistoquímica en sensibilidad y especificidad, esencial para el diagnóstico definitivo.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es la característica diagnóstica de la amiloidosis renal en la tinción con rojo Congo?
questions.explanation: La amiloidosis renal se caracteriza por depósito de material amiloide que tiñe con rojo Congo y muestra birrefringencia verde manzana bajo luz polarizada, hallazgo patognomónico.

questions.question: ¿Qué tipo de amiloide se deposita con mayor frecuencia en la amiloidosis renal primaria?
questions.explanation: La amiloidosis renal primaria (AL) se asocia a discrasias de células plasmáticas con depósito de cadenas ligeras, mientras que la AA se relaciona con inflamación crónica.

questions.question: ¿Qué hallazgo en microscopía electrónica confirma el diagnóstico de amiloidosis renal?
questions.explanation: La microscopía electrónica muestra fibrillas amiloides rígidas, no ramificadas, de 7-12 nm, características de la amiloidosis, a diferencia de otros depósitos glomerulares.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el tratamiento de primera línea en amiloidosis renal AL sintomática?
questions.explanation: La amiloidosis AL se trata con quimioterapia dirigida al clon de células plasmáticas, como melfalán más dexametasona o bortezomib, para reducir producción de cadenas ligeras.

questions.question: What renal manifestation is the most common in renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: La amiloidosis renal típicamente produce proteinuria masiva con síndrome nefrótico, debido al depósito de amiloide en glomérulos que altera la barrera de filtración.

questions.question: What additional stain helps differentiate AL amyloidosis from AA in renal biopsy?
questions.explanation: Immunohistochemistry with antibodies against kappa or lambda light chains allows typing AL amyloidosis, while AA is identified with anti-SAA.

questions.question: What is the most common stimulus for amyloid A formation in renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Amyloid A is an acute phase protein that is produced in excess in states of chronic inflammation, such as rheumatoid arthritis or tuberculosis, and its renal deposition causes AA amyloidosis.

questions.question: What precursor protein is deposited in renal amyloidosis associated with chronic inflammation?
questions.explanation: In AA amyloidosis, the precursor protein is serum amyloid A (SAA), an acute-phase apolipoprotein that is overproduced in chronic inflammation and misfolds to form amyloid fibrils.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism by which chronic inflammation induces AA amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation stimulates hepatic synthesis of serum amyloid A protein (SAA), which when partially degraded forms amyloid AA fibrils that are deposited in the kidney.

questions.question: What chronic disease is a common cause of renal AA amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is a classic cause of AA amyloidosis, as it produces chronic systemic inflammation that elevates SAA levels and promotes renal amyloid deposition.

questions.question: What is the characteristic histological finding in AA renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Renal amyloidosis is characterized by extracellular deposits of amorphous material that stain with Congo red and show apple-green birefringence under polarized light.

questions.question: What treatment is most effective for renal AA amyloidosis secondary to chronic inflammation?
questions.explanation: The main treatment of AA amyloidosis is to control the underlying inflammatory disease to reduce the production of SAA and thus stop the progression of kidney damage.

questions.question: What is the central pathophysiological mechanism in renal AL amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: In AL amyloidosis, monoclonal light chains produced by a plasmacytic clone fold abnormally and are deposited as amyloid fibrils in the kidney, causing glomerular and tubular damage.

questions.question: What is the most common clinical presentation of AL renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Renal AL amyloidosis typically manifests with nephrotic syndrome, proteinuria often >3 g/day, and progression to renal failure; macroscopic hematuria and severe HBP are less characteristic.

questions.question: Which renal biopsy finding is characteristic of AL amyloidosis?
options: Apple green tank with Congo red
questions.explanation: The amyloid deposit is evident with Congo red, showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light; The other findings correspond to other glomerulopathies.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el tratamiento de primera línea en amiloidosis AL renal?
questions.explanation: La terapia dirigida al clon plasmocitario con bortezomib más dexametasona (con o sin melfalán) es el estándar para reducir la producción de cadenas ligeras y preservar la función renal.

questions.question: What study confirms the monoclonal origin of AL amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Serum and urinary immunofixation detects free monoclonal light chains, essential to differentiate AL from other amyloidoses and guide oncohematological treatment.

questions.question: Which additional organ is most affected in AL amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: In addition to the kidney, the heart is the most frequently affected organ in AL, manifesting as restrictive heart failure and arrhythmias, which determines the prognosis.

questions.question: What is the most common clinical presentation of renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome is the most common presentation of renal amyloidosis, characterized by massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and edema.

questions.question: Which laboratory finding is characteristic of nephrotic syndrome?
questions.explanation: La proteinuria en rango nefrótico (>3.5 g/día) es el sello del síndrome nefrótico, junto con hipoalbuminemia y edema, secundario al depósito de amiloide.

questions.question: ¿Qué tipo de amiloide se deposita con mayor frecuencia en la amiloidosis renal primaria?
questions.explanation: La amiloidosis primaria (AL) se asocia a discrasias de células plasmáticas y depósito de cadenas ligeras, siendo la causa más común de afectación renal.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment for AL amyloidosis with kidney involvement?
questions.explanation: The bortezomib and dexamethasone regimen is the current standard for AL amyloidosis, aimed at eradicating the light chain-producing plasma clone.

questions.question: Which complication of nephrotic syndrome is most feared in renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: The hypercoagulability of nephrotic syndrome predisposes to renal vein thrombosis, a serious complication that can exacerbate renal dysfunction.

questions.question: ¿Qué tinción es la más utilizada para confirmar amiloide en biopsia renal?
questions.explanation: Congo red with apple green birefringence under polarized light is the standard technique for identifying amyloid deposits in kidney tissue.

questions.question: En la amiloidosis renal, la coexistencia de microhematuria e hipertensión arterial sugiere:
questions.explanation: La microhematuria glomerular y la hipertensión en amiloidosis renal indican depósito de amiloide en glomérulos y arteriolas, causando daño estructural y activación del sistema renina-angiotensina.

questions.question: What is the main mechanism of arterial hypertension in renal amyloidosis with microhematuria?
questions.explanation: The deposition of amyloid in renal arterioles, especially the afferent one, reduces renal blood flow and activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, raising blood pressure.

questions.question: Microhematuria in a patient with diagnosed renal amyloidosis should initially be interpreted as:
questions.explanation: La microhematuria glomerular es parte del espectro clínico de la amiloidosis renal, reflejando la lesión del filtro glomerular por depósitos de fibrillas amiloides.

questions.question: What histological finding explains the coexistence of microhematuria and hypertension in renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Amyloid deposition in the glomerular mesangium causes microhematuria, while arteriolar involvement produces ischemia and hypertension; both typically coexist.

questions.question: In renal amyloidosis with hypertension and microhematuria, which antihypertensive drug is especially indicated?
questions.explanation: ACEIs or ARBs are antihypertensive drugs of choice in renal proteinuria, including amyloidosis, due to their antiproteinuric and renoprotective effect in addition to pressure control.

questions.question: The appearance of de novo arterial hypertension in a patient with renal amyloidosis and microhematuria should alert us to:
questions.explanation: De novo hypertension in renal amyloidosis indicates greater vascular involvement by amyloid, which worsens the renal and cardiovascular prognosis, requiring therapeutic adjustment.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of enlarged kidneys in renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: The most common renal amyloidosis is the AL (light chain) type, which usually causes a diffuse increase in renal size on ultrasound due to amyloid deposition in the glomeruli and interstitium.

questions.question: In renal amyloidosis with enlarged kidneys, which additional sonographic finding is typical?
questions.explanation: In renal amyloidosis, the kidneys increase in size and show diffuse increase in cortical echogenicity due to amyloid infiltration, without characteristic cysts or stones.

questions.question: What pathophysiological mechanism explains the increase in kidney size in amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Amyloidosis is characterized by extracellular deposition of insoluble protein fibrils in glomeruli, vessels, and interstitium, which expands kidney tissue and increases its size.

questions.question: What test confirms the diagnosis of renal amyloidosis in a patient with enlarged kidneys?
options: Kidney biopsy with Congo red stain
questions.explanation: Renal biopsy with Congo red stain is the diagnostic standard; apple-green birefringence under polarized light confirms the presence of amyloid.

questions.question: What is the most common renal complication in amyloidosis with enlarged kidneys?
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome is the most common renal presentation of amyloidosis, due to diffuse glomerular involvement causing massive proteinuria.

questions.question: Which histologic finding is distinctive of renal amyloidosis in enlarged kidneys?
options: Amyloid fibrils in the mesangium and walls
questions.explanation: Amyloidosis shows deposition of amorphous eosinophilic material in the mesangium and capillary walls, which is identified as amyloid fibrils with electron microscopy and positive Congo red.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of renal amyloidosis with predominant glomerular involvement?
questions.explanation: AL (light chain) amyloidosis is the most common form of renal amyloidosis, typically depositing in the mesangium and glomerular basement membrane, while AA is more associated with chronic inflammation.

questions.question: What histological pattern is seen in amyloid glomerulopathy?
questions.explanation: Acellular nodular mesangial expansion with amyloid material is characteristic, and may be accompanied by deposits in the basement membrane, differentiating it from proliferative glomerulonephritis.

questions.question: What stain is essential to confirm amyloid deposit in kidney biopsy?
questions.explanation: Congo Red with apple green birefringence under polarized light is the classic technique to identify amyloid; the other stains are not specific for amyloid.

questions.question: What is the characteristic glomerular deposition in renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Amyloid accumulates mainly in the mesangium and along the glomerular basement membrane, producing thickening and disruption of the filtration barrier.

questions.question: What clinical feature is typical in advanced renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome with massive proteinuria is the most common manifestation, due to alteration of the glomerular basement membrane by amyloid deposits.

questions.question: What specific treatment is used in AL amyloidosis with kidney involvement?
questions.explanation: AL amyloidosis is treated with chemotherapy aimed at eradicating the light chain-producing clone, such as melphalan plus dexamethasone or bortezomib, not with anti-inflammatories.

questions.question: What laboratory technique is used to detect monoclonal protein in serum?
questions.explanation: Serum or urine protein electrophoresis is the initial test to detect a monoclonal protein, evidencing a monoclonal peak in the gamma region or other regions.

questions.question: In a patient with renal amyloidosis, the presence of monoclonal protein in urine is confirmed by:
questions.explanation: Immunofixation in urine is the confirmatory technique to identify the monoclonal light chain, especially when electrophoresis is inconclusive.

questions.question: What is the most common monoclonal light chain in primary renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: In primary AL amyloidosis, lambda light chain is observed in approximately 75% of cases, being more common than kappa.

questions.question: Which finding on serum electrophoresis suggests monoclonal protein?
questions.explanation: A monoclonal peak (narrow band) in the gamma region is the typical finding of a monoclonal protein on serum protein electrophoresis.

questions.question: What is the next test after detecting monoclonal protein in serum and urine in renal amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Biopsy of the affected tissue (kidney or abdominal fat) with Congo red stain is necessary to confirm the diagnosis of amyloidosis and type the deposit.

questions.question: In renal amyloidosis, the monoclonal protein may be negative in serum and urine in:
questions.explanation: In hereditary amyloidosis (ATTR), the monoclonal protein is usually absent, since the deposit is mutated transthyretin, not immunoglobulins.

questions.question: What is the first-line treatment for systemic AL amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Standard treatment for AL amyloidosis includes bortezomib-based chemotherapy combined with dexamethasone, achieving hematological and organ responses in many patients.

questions.question: What criteria contraindicate autologous stem cell transplantation in AL amyloidosis?
questions.explanation: Advanced cardiac amyloidosis (NYHA class III-IV) increases transplant mortality, which is why it is considered a relative or absolute contraindication for the procedure.

questions.question: What is the main objective of chemotherapy treatment in AL amyloidosis?
options: Eliminar el clon de células plasmáticas
questions.explanation: La terapia dirigida al clon de células plasmáticas productoras de cadenas ligeras es esencial, ya que al erradicar el clon se detiene la producción de amiloide y permite la reabsorción del depósito.

questions.question: ¿Qué agente se utiliza como terapia de consolidación antes del trasplante en AL?
questions.explanation: El bortezomib se emplea en esquemas de inducción para reducir la carga de cadenas ligeras antes del trasplante autólogo, mejorando la elegibilidad y los resultados del procedimiento.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es la respuesta hematológica deseada tras quimioterapia en AL?
options: Diferencia de cadenas ligeras menor a 40 mg/L
questions.explanation: Una respuesta hematológica óptima se define por la reducción de la diferencia entre cadenas ligeras libres (dFLC) a menos de 40 mg/L, lo que correlaciona con mejor supervivencia y recuperación orgánica.

questions.question: ¿Qué opción es un esquema de quimioterapia utilizado en amiloidosis AL?
questions.explanation: La combinación ciclofosfamida-bortezomib-dexametasona (CyBorD) es uno de los regímenes más utilizados en AL, mostrando altas tasas de respuesta hematológica y de órgano en la práctica clínica.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el tratamiento principal para la amiloidosis AA?
questions.explanation: AA amyloidosis is caused by deposition of serum amyloid A protein generated in chronic inflammatory processes; controlling the underlying disease reduces the inflammatory stimulus and stops the progression of amyloid deposit.

questions.question: ¿En qué contexto clínico se debe sospechar amiloidosis AA?
options: Paciente con artritis reumatoide y proteinuria
questions.explanation: La amiloidosis AA complica enfermedades inflamatorias crónicas como artritis reumatoide, espondilitis anquilosante o tuberculosis; la presencia de proteinuria en estos pacientes debe alertar sobre depósito renal de amiloide.

questions.question: ¿Qué estudio confirma el diagnóstico de amiloidosis renal?
options: Biopsia renal con tinción rojo Congo
questions.explanation: La biopsia renal con tinción rojo Congo es el estándar diagnóstico; muestra depósitos amiloides birrefringentes bajo luz polarizada. La inmunohistoquímica permite tipificar la proteína AA.

questions.question: ¿Qué proteína se deposita en la amiloidosis AA?
questions.explanation: La amiloidosis AA se caracteriza por depósito de fragmentos de la proteína amiloide A sérica, una reactante de fase aguda producida en hígado ante estímulos inflamatorios crónicos; su control es terapéutico clave.

questions.question: ¿Qué manifestación renal es la más frecuente en amiloidosis AA?
questions.explanation: El depósito glomerular de amiloide AA produce proteinuria progresiva, a menudo en rango nefrótico (mayor a 3.5 g/día), con hipoalbuminemia y edema; la hematuria macroscópica es infrecuente.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el pronóstico renal si se controla la enfermedad inflamatoria base?
questions.explanation: El control de la enfermedad base reduce el sustrato amiloide, pudiendo estabilizar o incluso mejorar la proteinuria y la función renal; el pronóstico renal depende de la remisión inflamatoria.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es la terapia de elección inicial en enfermedad renal terminal por amiloidosis renal?
questions.explanation: El trasplante renal es la terapia de elección en pacientes con enfermedad renal terminal por amiloidosis renal, siempre que la enfermedad de base esté controlada y no existan contraindicaciones, ya que ofrece mejor supervivencia y calidad de vida que las modalidades dialíticas.

questions.question: ¿Qué modalidad dialítica se prefiere en pacientes con amiloidosis renal y disfunción autonómica severa?
questions.explanation: La diálisis peritoneal automatizada se prefiere en pacientes con disfunción autonómica severa porque los cambios hemodinámicos son más graduales y mejor tolerados que la hemodiálisis, que puede provocar hipotensión intradiálisis.

questions.question: ¿Qué factor contraindica el trasplante renal en un paciente con amiloidosis renal?
questions.explanation: La amiloidosis activa sistémica contraindica el trasplante renal porque la enfermedad puede recurrir en el injerto y comprometer su supervivencia; se debe lograr remisión o control de la enfermedad de base antes de considerar el trasplante.

questions.question: ¿Cuál es el principal riesgo al usar furosemida en pacientes con amiloidosis renal en diálisis?
questions.explanation: La furosemida en pacientes en diálisis puede causar hipotensión intradiálisis, especialmente en aquellos con disfunción autonómica por amiloidosis, ya que reduce el volumen plasmático y puede exacerbar la inestabilidad hemodinámica durante la sesión.

questions.question: ¿Qué hallazgo de laboratorio es característico en la enfermedad renal terminal por amiloidosis renal?
questions.explanation: La proteinuria masiva con cociente albumina/creatinina elevado es característica de la afectación renal por amiloidosis, que progresa a enfermedad renal terminal; los otros hallazgos son menos específicos o de otras etiologías.

questions.question: En paciente con amiloidosis renal terminal, ¿cuál es la primera línea para controlar la proteinuria antes de diálisis?
questions.explanation: Los inhibidores de la enzima convertidora de angiotensina (IECA) son la primera línea para controlar la proteinuria en enfermedad renal crónica, incluyendo la amiloidosis renal, ya que reducen la presión intraglomerular y la excreción de proteínas.
